note: The same night in John: he says his followers would fight if his kingdom were from here, and when Peter does fight, he stops him.
Twice in John a kingship is pressed on him by force, by a crowd and then by the charge before Pilate, and twice he declines the means.
Both are said to Pilate: his kingdom does not come from here, and Pilate's power comes from above.
The same trial: Pilate's claim to power over life and death is the setting for the answer about a kingdom not from here.
Consecutive verses. Pilate claims the power to free or crucify; Jesus says that power was given.
The two Gospel forms of the sword put away at the arrest; Matthew adds the angels he does not call.
Luke's arrest: the disciples ask whether to strike, one does, and Jesus stops it and heals the wound.
Two responses to the drawn sword: the force he declines, and the injury he undoes.
Consecutive verses: the kingdoms shown, then the price named.
The same temptation in Matthew and Luke. Luke alone has the devil's claim that the authority was handed to him.
Two claims about who hands out authority, the devil's in the wilderness and Jesus' before Pilate. The texts do not set them side by side; this reading does.
The devil says the kingdoms are his to give to whoever he likes; Daniel's decree says the Most High gives them to whom he wills. The claims compete.
The offer of the kingdoms set against Daniel's claim of who gives them. A reading across the canon.
The mock king: purple and thorns from the soldiers, the title on the cross from Pilate.
The same chapter of John: the placard names him King of the Jews just after the priests claim the emperor as their only king.
Revelation's opening title for Jesus, ruler over earth's kings, is cashed out when the Lamb conquers the kings as King of kings.
The elder announces a lion, and John turns and sees a slaughtered lamb. The victory is announced in one image and shown in the other.
The lamb that was slaughtered in Revelation, and Isaiah's servant led like a lamb to slaughter.
Revelation's own link: the believers win by the Lamb's blood, the Lamb who won by being slaughtered.
A kingdom not from this world, and one that does not come in ways that can be watched for. Both say what the kingdom is not.
The crowd wants to make him king by force; Israel wanted a king to fight its battles. Both want a king who acts like the nations' kings.
At the arrest Jesus does what he taught: he does not resist the one doing evil.
He sheathes the sword to drink the cup, the life given as ransom of Matthew 20:28.
His kingdom does not come from here, and it is not run as the nations' rulers run theirs.
The conquering lamb and Zechariah's king who removes the chariot and the warhorse. A reading, not a citation.
Jesus heals the enemy's wound at the arrest; Elisha feeds the enemy's army. Both answer force with care.
The legions of angels Jesus does not call, and the one angel who struck Assyria's camp. The power exists; he declines it.
Consecutive in the story: the killing and God's question about the blood.
Lamech's song in two verses: the killing, then the boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge.
Lamech's seventy-seven for vengeance, and Jesus' seventy-seven for forgiveness. Many readers see the reversal; the Gospel does not cite Genesis.
Jesus names Abel's blood explicitly.
Hebrews names Abel's blood explicitly and sets Jesus' blood against it.
Both name Abel's blood. Matthew's is the start of a line of murdered righteous people, and Hebrews' is answered by better blood.
Blood that cries from the ground, and blood that defiles the land: both say spilled blood stays on the land.
Both put blood for blood into law: the life of the one who kills answers for the life taken.
The flood comes on an earth full of violence, and the law of blood is given immediately after it.
Nimrod's kingdom begins at Babel (Genesis 10:10), and the Babel story follows. The first warrior and the first city built to make a name.
Consecutive verses: wars come from desires within, and desire unsatisfied ends in killing.
James describes what Cain did: wanting, not getting, killing.
Two family boasts of violence in Genesis, Lamech's and the brothers' swords at Shechem. The thread is drawn here.
The law that blood answers for blood, and Revelation's version: whoever kills by the sword dies by it.
Both are from the same chapter: a king like the nations', who goes out and fights.
God's answer to the elders' request: they have rejected him as king.
Gideon refuses to rule because God rules; in Samuel the people reverse it, and God reads their choice as rejecting him.
Jotham's fable: the trees ask the useful plants first, and only the bramble accepts.
Jotham's fable is told against Abimelech, Gideon's son, who took the kingship Gideon had refused.
Judges ends with no king and each person doing what seemed right to himself; Samuel opens with the request for one. The canon's order joins them.
Hosea says the later kings were made without God's choice or knowledge. The rejection in 1 Samuel 8 continues.
The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17: limits on horses and the copy of the law.
The purpose of the copy: that the king not raise himself above his kin.
The king is not to send to Egypt for horses, and Isaiah condemns those who rely on Egypt's horses.
The people want a king to fight their battles; David tells Goliath that the fight belongs to God.
Samuel's rebuke is about Saul's sparing of the spoil, the same chapter.
Pharaoh's two orders, to the midwives in secret and then to all his people in public.
The order and the refusal: the midwives fear God and disobey it.
Two kings order the killing of boys. Matthew's birth story is often read against Exodus; Matthew does not cite the Nile order directly.
Two kings who set their own word against God's: Pharaoh asks who the LORD is, Nebuchadnezzar commands worship of his statue.
The furnace decree and the three men's answer to it.
The decree and the refusal: they will not bow, even if God does not save them.
A law forbidding prayer to anyone but the king, and the apostles' rule that God is obeyed over men.
Esther: the decree to destroy, and the rule that a sealed royal order cannot be revoked. The king cannot undo his own law, only issue another.
Isaiah's woe in two verses: the unjust decree, and whom it robs.
Laws that make widows and orphans prey, and Jeremiah's command not to wrong them.
Jezebel takes the vineyard by a judicial murder; Elijah's sentence on Ahab follows in the same chapter.
An empire's sealed decree to destroy a people, set against the claim that authorities are instituted by God. The tension is drawn here, not in either text.
The same war: David stays home while Joab besieges Rabbah, and Uriah dies at Rabbah's wall.
Conquerors who humiliate captured kings. Adoni-bezek says God repaid him as he had done.
Adoni-bezek's own verdict, as I did, so God repaid me, is Revelation's rule applied to one man.
Both name the ripping open of pregnant women as a conqueror's act, Hazael in Kings and Ammon in Amos.
Two kings who credit their own strength: Assyria's I have done it, Babylon's I have built.
Assyria credits its own hand, and the Chaldeans make their own strength their god.
Consecutive verses in the siege of Samaria.
The siege of Samaria fulfils what the covenant curse foretold.
The same curse fulfilled in Jerusalem's fall.
The law of war in Deuteronomy 20: offer peace first; spare the trees in a siege.
Two failures over the spoil: Achan takes it and hides it, Saul keeps the best of it.
Abram refuses a thread of the spoils; Achan covets and buries them. Set side by side here.
Nahum's woe: the bloody city, then the battlefield.
Corpses beyond counting in Nahum and bodies left unburied like sheaves in Jeremiah.
The valley of bones, then the breath called into the slain.
The unburied slain of Jeremiah and the valley of the slain in Ezekiel. The thread is drawn here; Ezekiel is told the bones are the whole house of Israel (37:11).
A king made to watch his sons killed, and the sword that never leaves David's house. Two royal houses broken by the sword.
Consecutive verses: the call to the birds and what they are called to eat.
Revelation's supper of the birds is built on Ezekiel's: the bodies of the mighty and the blood of princes.
The red horse takes peace from the earth, and Jesus says wars will come but are not the end.
The same scene in Revelation 19: the kings gathered for war become the birds' supper.
Nathan's charge and the sentence that follows from it.
The sword stays in David's house, and David is barred from building God's house because of the blood he shed.
Naboth's blood answered on Ahab, as Abel's blood cried out against Cain.
In Revelation the one who kills by the sword is killed by it, and Babylon, holding the blood of the slaughtered, falls.
Both describe Babylon in Revelation as full of the saints' blood.
Abner's question about kin chasing kin, and the first killing of a brother. The thread is drawn here.
Both say a king's army and horses are not what saves.
Consecutive verses: not the army, not the warhorse.
Trust in horses and chariots rather than in God is the charge in both.
Isaiah condemns relying on horses; Hosea says God will save without them.
Not by bow, sword or horses in Hosea; not by might or power in Zechariah.
Victory belongs to God in both, said by David to Goliath and in Proverbs.
The same sentence spoken over two battles: the battle is God's.
At the sea and before Jehoshaphat's battle, the people are told God fights for them.
The same event: the promise that God will fight, then the song that he is a warrior.
The LORD as warrior, and the LORD who trains David's hands for war. These pull against the passages where God saves without weapons; both are in the text.
Psalm 144 thanks God for training David for war; 1 Samuel 17 has the same David say God saves without sword or spear. The tension is the text's own.
Horses and chariots, Judah's trust in Isaiah, are what God's sword is against in Jeremiah.
Not by might but by my spirit, and weapons that are not merely human.
The warhorse is a false hope, and the coming king cuts off the warhorse.
The decree that God rules human kingdoms, and the boast that proves its point, in the same chapter.
Two Babylonian kings in Daniel: the boast and the verdict.
God names a foreign king his servant and another his anointed. Both are instruments; neither is the one who rules.
Daniel says God gives kingdoms to whom he will; Jeremiah shows him giving them to Nebuchadnezzar.
Kings reign through wisdom in Proverbs, and by the Most High's grant in Daniel.
Two angels strike a king's power: Assyria's army in a night and Herod's body in public.
Herod takes God's glory and falls; Nebuchadnezzar takes credit for Babylon and falls.
God brings down the powerful and lifts the lowly, and he sets the lowliest over kingdoms.
Psalm 2: the kings rage, and heaven laughs.
Psalm 2 continues: the anointed breaks them.
Psalm 2 ends with the warning to the kings: be wise.
Acts 4 quotes Psalm 2 and applies it to the plot against Jesus.
Isaiah 14's taunt: the fall and the boast that caused it.
The same taunt: the one who would sit above the stars is stared at in his grave.
Babel's tower reaching heaven and the king who would climb above God's stars. Both build upward to make a name.
The one who brought nations down is brought down; God pulls rulers off their thrones.
The kings who hide in caves in Revelation and the fallen king the dead stare at. Drawn here.
Revelation 19:15 takes up Psalm 2's iron rod. Cross-topic link to Swords & Words, where the verse sits as the sword from the mouth.
The Teacher's two observations: oppressors hold power, and one person rules another to his hurt.
A chain of officials each over another, and power used by one person over another to his harm.
Micah's charge in two verses: the rulers who strip and devour the people.
Rulers who eat the people in Micah, officials who tear them as wolves in Ezekiel.
Ezekiel's two pictures of rulers: shepherds who rule by force, officials who prey like wolves.
Two proverbs on rule: the wicked ruler is a beast to the poor, and the people groan under him.
Do justice and do no violence, in Jeremiah to the king, and in Micah to every person.
The king as he should be: defender of the poor, reigning in righteousness.
Shepherds who ruled by force and the nations' rulers who lord it over them. Jesus does not cite Ezekiel.
John tells soldiers not to extort; Jesus tells his hearers not to resist the evildoer. Two teachings about force, to different people.
One person over another to his hurt, and rulers who lord it over the nations: the same observation, made centuries apart.
The king who defends the poor, and the servant who will not break the bruised reed.
Consecutive verses: the rulers of the nations, then not so among you.
The reason given: he himself came to serve.
The same saying in Matthew and Mark.
The same saying in Matthew and Luke. Luke sets it at the Last Supper and adds the title benefactors.
Luke's form continues: the leader as one who serves.
The Philippians hymn: emptied, then humbled to the cross.
The Son of Man gives his life; the one in God's form obeys to death.
Isaiah 42: no shouting, no breaking of the reed, and justice all the same.
Zechariah 9: the king arrives on a donkey, and removes the instruments of war.
Matthew quotes Zechariah 9:9 at the entry into Jerusalem.
The servant is silent before his shearers, and Jesus is silent before Pilate. John does not cite Isaiah here.
The king removes chariot and bow, and the nations hammer swords into farm tools: the same end of war, by different hands.
The leader as a servant, and the king who must not raise himself above his kin.
Jesus quotes the eye-for-eye law.
Consecutive verses: you have heard, but I say.
The Sermon's two answers to an enemy: do not resist and love.
Love of neighbour in Leviticus is extended to love of enemy in Matthew.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35.
Romans 12: repay no one evil; leave room for God's wrath.
Romans 12 ends: overcome evil with good.
Peter describes Christ suffering without threat, and Luke shows him praying for those who crucify him.
Luke wrote both. Stephen dies as Jesus died, praying for those killing him.
Consecutive verses: the request for fire and the rebuke.
Elisha's feast for the enemy army, and its result: the raids stop.
Evil overcome with good: the raiding army fed, and the raids end.
Elisha feeds the captured enemy; Jesus says to love the enemy.
David spares Saul and leaves judgement to God.
Joseph does not take revenge on his brothers, and God turns the harm to good. Paul does not cite Joseph.
Like for like limits revenge; Lamech's seventy-seven had no limit. Many readers take the law as a curb on revenge; the text does not say so.
The fire the disciples want to call down, and the bramble king's threat of fire. The thread is drawn here.
God takes vengeance, and God fights for his people. In both, the force belongs to God and not to them.
Isaiah and Micah share almost the same oracle word for word.
Joel reverses the plowshares oracle, turning tools into weapons for the day of judgement.
God breaks the bow and ends war in both.
Two psalms of God breaking the weapons: bow and spear, arrows and sword.
Isaiah 9: the child's names and his peace without end.
The Prince of Peace and the humble king on the donkey, two pictures of a king without warfare.
A season for war, and wars that must come but are not the end. The thread is drawn here.
Self-control beats taking a city; wisdom beats weapons.
The same passage: the poor wise man saved the city, and wisdom beats weapons.
A city saved by wisdom; a city taken by force is worth less than self-control.
Romans 13: authorities instituted by God; the ruler bears the sword as God's servant.
Two answers to the same council in Acts: we must obey God.
The two sayings held in tension. Romans tells everyone to submit; Acts says God is obeyed first when the two conflict. Neither cancels the other in the text.
Pilate's power was given from above, and every authority exists by God's appointment. Both affirm the grant; neither says it is used well.
The midwives and the three men in the furnace both refuse a king's order to God's honour.
Consecutive verses: God can save us, and even if he does not.
Praying for kings and submitting to them in Paul's letters.
In Romans 12 vengeance is God's, and in Romans 13 the ruler executes God's wrath. Paul places the sword with the ruler and not with the believer.
The priests' only king is the emperor, and Israel had rejected God as king. A reading across the canon; John does not cite Samuel.
Gamaliel's counsel in Acts 5.
Gamaliel's two examples: movements that rose by force and scattered when their leader died.
The test in two halves: of human origin it fails, of God it cannot be overthrown.
The examples lead to the counsel: leave them alone.
No counsel succeeds against the LORD, and a work of God cannot be overthrown.
Psalm 33: the nations' plans frustrated and God's counsel standing.
God's counsel stands and his purpose is established.
God's purpose stands, and who can turn back his hand?
Daniel 2: the stone, then its meaning, a kingdom that ends the others.
Daniel 2's kingdom never destroyed, and Daniel 7's dominion that will not pass.
A stone cut without hands, and a work not of human origin. Gamaliel does not cite Daniel; the link is drawn here.
Mark's time fulfilled, and Paul's time come to its fullness.
An appointed time that will not delay, and a time that came to fullness.
The vision awaits its time, and in its time God will hasten it.
An everlasting dominion given to one like a son of man, and the world's kingdom become the Messiah's.
The struggle is not against flesh and blood, and its weapons are not merely human.
The rulers who crucified him, unknowing, and the rulers disarmed at the cross.
Paul twice in 1 Corinthians: rulers of this age who did not understand, and every ruler destroyed at the end.
The Lamb conquers, and those with him conquer by his blood and their testimony.
Kings gathered for war against the Lamb or the rider in Revelation 17 and 19.
Luke 17: not observed; among you.
A kingdom the violent try to seize, and a kingdom that cannot be watched for or pointed to. The saying in Matthew 11:12 is disputed; the link is a reading.
Judas of Galilee rose up at the census; Israel asked for a king to fight. Two attempts to win freedom by force. Drawn here.
Theudas gathered four hundred and died; the crowd wanted to make Jesus king and he withdrew. Gamaliel's examples are the kind of movement Jesus refused to lead.
The kings of Psalm 2 rage against God and his anointed; the kingdom becomes the anointed's in Revelation 11. Revelation 11:18 alludes to the raging nations.
Every ruler destroyed at the end, and rulers brought down from thrones.
The ruler's sword and the believer's weapons that are not merely human, two kinds of force Paul names in two letters.
No counsel against the LORD, and the Most High rules over human kingdoms.
A kingdom not from this world, and the kingdom the God of heaven sets up, which ends the others.
His kingdom does not fight, and Gamaliel says a work of God need not be fought for, since it cannot be overthrown. Drawn here.
